content_voiceover: This slide walks through the full pathway from fibrinogen to a stable cross-linked clot, using a simplified D, E, D cartoon instead of the detailed chain diagram. Starting at the top, fibrinogen has that central E domain flanked by two D domains, and thrombin, factor two a, cleaves off fibrinopeptides A and B to produce fibrin monomer. Right now the highlighted step is that very first conversion, fibrinogen to fibrin monomer. Once the fibrinopeptides are gone, the newly exposed E domain of one monomer can bind the D domain of an adjacent monomer, and monomers start to self assemble in a half staggered, overlapping arrangement, which is what eventually builds the fibrin polymer you see below, still dimmed at this point in the animation. Then factor thirteen gets activated by thrombin into factor thirteen a, a transglutaminase that will cross-link the polymer into its final stable form, but that part comes later in the sequence. The key takeaway from this frame is that thrombin's proteolytic action on fibrinogen is what generates fibrin monomer, the basic building block of the clot.
keypoints: Full pathway shown: fibrinogen to monomer to polymer to cross-linked fibrin
Thrombin (IIa) cleaves FPA and FPB to generate fibrin monomer, highlighted step
Exposed E domain binds D domain of adjacent monomer for self-assembly
Factor XIII is activated by thrombin to factor XIIIa, a transglutaminase
Cross-linking by FXIIIa is the final stabilization step, shown later
keypoint_voiceover: This is the whole cascade at a glance, fibrinogen to monomer to polymer to cross-linked fibrin. Right now we're focused on step one, thrombin cleaving fibrinopeptides A and B to make fibrin monomer, which then self-assembles by D domain to E domain contacts. Factor thirteen a will cross-link that polymer later.
